hints: Handle one block at a time. Before reversing a block, what must you check, and what four links must be fixed after reversing it?

Iterative group reversal with a dummy node. Keep groupPrev (the tail of the previous finished block). Check that k nodes exist ahead, reverse exactly those k with the prev/cur loop, then reconnect both ends.

1. Make dummy → head; groupPrev = dummy.
  2. Find kth by walking k steps from groupPrev; if it runs out, stop.
  3. Remember groupNext = kth.next; reverse nodes from groupPrev.next up to kth, with prev starting at groupNext.
  4. Link groupPrev.next = kth; the old block start is now its tail, so set groupPrev to it.
  5. Repeat; return dummy.next.

approaches.name: Use a stack / array
approaches.idea: Push k nodes onto a stack and pop them to relink each block. Simple but needs O(k) memory.

approaches.name: Recursive
approaches.idea: Reverse the first k, recurse on the rest; uses O(n/k) call stack.

approaches.name: Optimal: iterative in-place reversal
approaches.idea: Reverse each complete block with pointers only.

explain: For 1→…→8 with k = 3: the first block 1,2,3 becomes 3→2→1 and 1 links to the rest; the second block becomes 6→5→4; only 7 and 8 remain, fewer than 3, so they stay. The result is 3,2,1,6,5,4,7,8. Starting prev at groupNext means the reversed block's tail already points to what follows. With k = 1 every block is a single node and nothing changes.
recognize: Reverse a linked list in fixed-size chunks, leaving a short tail alone → check k ahead, reverse k in place, reconnect, move on.
javascript: function reverseKGroup(head, k) { const a = []; for (let c = head; c; c = c.next) a.push(c); const b = []; for (let i = 0; i < a.length; i += k) { const blk = a.slice(i, i + k); b.push(...(blk.length === k ? blk.reverse() : blk)); } for (let i = 0; i < b.length; i++) b[i].next = b[i+1] || null; return b[0] || null; }
